workshops.title: Swift workbench: predict a result, then check it
workshops.summary: Run a small Swift program on your computer. Check how lists keep order, repeated topics add up, copied values change, and tests explain a wrong answer.

simple.story: You keep a notebook of study sessions. One page says Swift, 20 minutes. Another says Actors, 15 minutes. A third says Swift, 10 minutes. You can read the pages in their original order, or add the minutes for each topic. Those are two different questions about the same notebook. When you add an Actors page with 5 minutes, the reading order gains one page. The Actors total becomes 20 minutes. Writing the expected answers first lets you check your work.
simple.meaning: The Swift package turns small input lists into labels, totals, and distinct topics. Each function promises a particular result and order. A host test compares that promise with what the program returns.

example.before: The positive readings are Swift 20, Actors 15, and Swift 10. A fourth reading, Skipped 0, is also in the input.
example.change: Append Reading(topic: "Actors", minutes: 5) to the fixture.
example.after: Labels end with Actors: 5. Alphabetical totals are Actors 20 and Swift 30. Distinct topics remain Actors, Skipped, Swift because Skipped is still present and Actors was already a member.

picture.caption: One added reading changes labels and totals, while topic membership stays the same.

items.label: Four readings
items.text: The input includes three positive readings and Skipped 0.

items.label: Add Actors 5
items.text: Append one reading to the end of the input.

items.label: Check labels
items.text: Positive readings keep their input order and gain Actors: 5.

items.label: Check totals and topics

words.meaning: The computer running this package, rather than an iOS app destination.
Small chosen inputs with independently known expected results.
A test check that reports when an actual result differs from the expected result.
Copied values can change independently, even when their storage is shared internally.
Code that works with a caller-chosen type under stated requirements.

simple.remember: Predict values, order, and membership separately before running the test.
simple.boundary: The notebook explains collection results. It does not explain memory allocation. Swift value copying can share array storage internally, and a copied struct can still contain a reference to the same class object. Passing host tests supplies no app or device evidence.

sections.title: Run the package on your computer
sections.html:
A host program runs on your computer. This workshop uses one to learn Swift before adding an iOS screen. SwiftPM, the Swift Package Manager, builds three parts from separate directories: a library, a command-line program, and tests. The library product is SwiftLanguageLab; the executable product is swift-workbench. If you have built a small JVM command-line project, that division will feel familiar. Run the program and check its answers before dealing with Xcode destinations, signing, or view lifetime. All inputs are invented practice values. The package imports no company client and contacts no service. Its results are evidence about this host program.

Open the supplied Package.swift first. Its tools-version comment selects the minimum SwiftPM tools contract, while swiftLanguageModes selects Swift 6 language checking. The macOS platform entry is a deployment floor, not a promise that the oldest operating system includes your compiler. dependencies is empty: Swift Testing comes from the installed toolchain, so there is no remote testing package to fetch. Author verification used Apple Swift 6.4 on macOS; a Swift 6.0 compiler and Linux were not executed. Record your own version rather than treating that observation as your environment.

From the course directory, enter labs/SwiftLanguageLab and reproduce the isolated-cache shell function in the supplied README. It creates a unique directory beneath /private/tmp, passes SwiftPM scratch, package cache, configuration, and security paths, and sets the compiler module cache paths. The two-job setting limits build pressure. Keep the same shell open so the lab_swift function and lab_cache variable still exist. These commands then build the examples, execute them, and discover the language tests:

swift --version
lab_swift run swift-workbench language
lab_swift test --filter LanguageTests

Read Sources/SwiftWorkbench/main.swift as the executable entry. import makes another module's public declarations available. @main identifies its entry type; static func main is the entry function. Its async throws declaration permits awaiting gates and propagating fixture failures in the other modes. A top-level failure is not silently converted into success. Sessions 057–060 supply the first-program, type, flow, and function vocabulary; sessions 067 and 068 explain errors and closures. This package supplies host execution evidence, while a future native workshop supplies app execution evidence.

sections.title: Check list order, totals, and missing numbers
sections.html:
A collection is a group of values, such as four study readings. A contract states what a function must return from that group. Read LanguageExamples.swift beside LanguageTests.swift so you can compare each promise with its checks. Reading is an immutable struct: its topic and minutes fields cannot change after creation. It has an explicit public initializer so another module can create a Reading; Swift does not automatically expose the generated memberwise initializer publicly. In labels(for: readings), for is an argument label required by that function's declaration. This differs from choosing Kotlin named arguments at a call site. The example below uses the actual public API inside a function or the program entry point.

let readings = [
    Reading(topic: "Swift", minutes: 20),
    Reading(topic: "Actors", minutes: 15),
    Reading(topic: "Swift", minutes: 10),
    Reading(topic: "Skipped", minutes: 0)
]
let labels = LanguageExamples.labels(for: readings)
let totals = LanguageExamples.totalsByTopic(readings)
let topics = LanguageExamples.distinctTopics(readings)

labels first filters positive minutes, then maps surviving entries into strings. The expected sequence is Swift: 20, Actors: 15, Swift: 10. filter and map retain array encounter order. The zero-minute item disappears here, but distinctTopics includes its topic: deduplication and positive-minute filtering are different policies. A Kotlin filter followed by map offers a familiar conceptual bridge, while Swift closure parameter shorthand $0 and argument labels require their own explanation.

totalsByTopic accumulates in a dictionary using its default-value subscript. A missing topic starts at zero before adding minutes. Repeated Swift entries produce thirty minutes. The function sorts keys before returning named tuples, giving the display an explicit alphabetical contract. Dictionary and Set iteration are not a sorting policy. A test that only checks the number of rows would miss a reordered or incorrectly accumulated result. Named tuple fields permit totals.map(\.topic), where the key-path expression selects a property from each element.

parsePresentIntegers uses compactMap: Int conversion returns an optional, and nil conversions disappear. The malformed input bad does not become zero and does not throw. firstEvenSquare uses lazy filtering and mapping to obtain the first qualifying result; it does not evaluate or cache every transformed value. Optional nil represents no matching result. The square calculation accepts small fixtures; Int overflow is not a general numeric-domain policy. Sessions 061–063 cover arrays, sets, dictionaries, transformations, and lazy iteration. Predict both values and ordering before running, and distinguish an intentional lossy transformation from validation that must report bad input.

sections.title: Copy a plan and check what is shared
sections.html:
A value copy lets you change one plan without changing the other. ReadingPlan stores an array of topics. Other modules can read its topics, but its restricted setter prevents them from replacing the array directly. The append method is marked mutating because it changes this struct's value. Start with Swift in both plans, append Actors to the copy, and append Files to the original. Each plan keeps its own visible result. Swift arrays may share internal storage until a change needs separate storage; this is called copy-on-write. These checks prove the value behavior. They do not count allocations or show how many bytes were copied.

var original = ReadingPlan(topics: ["Swift"])
var copy = original
copy.append("Actors")
original.append("Files")
// original.topics is ["Swift", "Files"]
// copy.topics is ["Swift", "Actors"]

var source = 10
var destination = 4
LanguageExamples.transfer(3, from: &source, to: &destination)

The ampersand at an inout argument grants temporary mutable access, not a general-purpose address you may retain. transfer needs two nonoverlapping accesses. Passing the same variable to both arguments violates that requirement; do not run that as if Swift promised an atomic self-transfer. The worked input satisfies the function's preconditions and leaves both values at seven. Preconditions identify unsupported inputs; they are not recoverable validation errors. Sessions 064 and 065 connect mutation, exclusivity, properties, initialization, and access control.

Copy CounterEnvelope next. It is a struct containing a ReferenceCounter class. The copied envelopes still refer to the same counter, so mutating that object is visible through both. The identity operator === answers whether two class references identify the same object; == answers a value equality contract when available. A Kotlin data class holding a mutable collection has a similar shallow-copy trap, but Swift struct assignment and Kotlin copy are different mechanisms. ReferenceCounter deliberately does not claim Sendable, because unrestricted shared mutable state would not become safe merely by wrapping it in a struct.

Stack<Element: Sendable> is generic: the caller chooses an element type satisfying the constraint, and push and pop retain that type. pop returns Element? because an empty stack is valid. LessonLabel is a protocol requiring readable text. renderedLabel preserves a generic concrete parameter, makeLabel returns some LessonLabel hiding one fixed implementation type, and renderLabels accepts an array of any LessonLabel so different conforming types can coexist. some is not a runtime choice among arbitrary unrelated implementations; any is an existential storage contract. The tests add a second label type to prove heterogeneity. Sessions 066–069 cover class relationships, errors, capture lifetime, and generic boundaries; inheritance and closure ownership still require their numbered exercises beyond this package's selected examples.

sections.title: Read a failed check, then extend the fixture
sections.html:
An assertion compares a program's result with an expected answer. Swift Testing finds functions marked @Test. It does not use XCTest's test-method naming rule. These suites import SwiftLanguageLab's public API; they do not use @testable to reach private state. #expect reports a failed check and allows later checks to continue. try #require stops that test when a required condition fails, or unwraps an optional needed by later work. Tests may run at the same time, so each language test owns its fixture. The file tests own separate directories, and the concurrency tests own separate actors. This separation keeps tests independent without requiring a serial run.

After a successful baseline, deliberately replace the expected parsePresentIntegers array with [10, 0, -2], run the language suite, and read the issue. This exact teaching mutation was executed during author verification: the focused run exited with a failure and displayed an actual result of [10, -2]. That is consistent with compactMap dropping nil conversions. Restore the expectation immediately. The shipped expectation is the correct one; the deliberate failure is a diagnostic exercise, not an unresolved defect or evidence that the learner has completed it.

For a meaningful new exercise, add Reading(topic: "Actors", minutes: 5) to the collection fixture. Calculate expected labels, sorted totals, and distinct topics on paper. The additional reading appears at the end of labels because that operation retains input order. Actors accumulates twenty minutes; Swift remains thirty. The distinct topic sequence does not gain another Actors entry. Change those expectations deliberately and run the focused suite, then the full suite. If an assertion fails, identify whether membership, value, or ordering differs. Do not rewrite the expected value by calling the same aggregation algorithm inside the test.

A compiler diagnostic about mutation of a let binding happens before tests can run. An assertion issue points at a violated fixture expectation after the program ran. A build-environment problem may involve unavailable toolchain components or cache paths and needs its own fix. Session 012 teaches the framework distinction, and session 070 integrates retrieval and independent explanation. Passing the instructor tests establishes that the shipped examples behave under the recorded host conditions. Your exercise needs your changed fixture, command, result, and explanation. The course records no automatic completion or certification from this package.

exercise.brief: Run the language examples. Make one expected answer wrong, explain the failure, and restore it. Then add an Actors reading and check copying and generic types.
steps: Follow the README's isolated-cache setup. Record swift --version, then run swift-workbench language and the LanguageTests suite.
Write the labels, alphabetically ordered totals, and distinct topics you expect from the four readings before reading the assertions.
Temporarily change the parsePresentIntegers expectation to [10, 0, -2]. Run the focused suite, explain why bad adds no zero, and restore [10, -2].
Add Reading(topic: "Actors", minutes: 5). Write the new labels and totals yourself; explain why the distinct topic list stays the same.
Predict both copied ReadingPlan arrays and the shared CounterEnvelope counter. Run the checks and explain why inout needs separate mutable arguments.
In a scratch exercise, push 3 and 8 onto Stack<Int> and pop three times. Explain the generic type, any LessonLabel, and some LessonLabel.
Restore every deliberate failure and run the full instructor suite. Record your own changed fixture, commands, results, and explanation.
acceptance: The toolchain, isolated cache setup, executed commands, and actual exit statuses are recorded.
The modified collection fixture proves Actors totals twenty and Swift thirty, with alphabetical totals and encounter-order labels.
The deliberate failure is explained and restored; malformed numeric input is not silently redefined as zero.
Value copying is distinguished from shared nested class identity without invented allocation measurements.
Public generic and optional contracts are explained; passing instructor tests does not mark learner work complete.
exercise.solution:
The added Actors reading contributes 5 minutes. Labels now read Swift: 20, Actors: 15, Swift: 10, Actors: 5, in that order. Alphabetical totals are Actors 20 and Swift 30. distinctTopics stays Actors, Skipped, Swift: Skipped remains in the input even though it has no positive minutes, and Actors was already present. Write these answers from the small inputs. Calling the same aggregation function to create a test's expected value would repeat its possible mistake.

var stack = Stack<Int>()
stack.push(3)
stack.push(8)
let last = stack.pop() // Optional(8)
let earlier = stack.pop() // Optional(3)
let empty = stack.pop() // nil

The concrete element type is Int throughout, and nil is an ordinary empty-stack result. The copying exercise gives original Swift/Files and copy Swift/Actors, while both CounterEnvelope values observe the same counter mutation. The deliberately incorrect parse expectation fails because bad converts to nil and compactMap omits it. Restore that expectation before assessing new changes. Capture your own run; the worked answer describes the intended behavior but does not create your fixture, pre-complete your exercise, or make a claim about an iOS app.

quiz.question: What does a passing ReadingPlan copying test establish?
options: The copied plans can change independently according to the value contract.
Every assignment eagerly allocates a new array buffer.
Any struct deeply copies objects reachable from its properties.
quiz.explanation: The assertions observe independent values. Copy-on-write may share internal storage until needed, and nested class references keep their identity; no allocation measurement occurred.

quiz.question: Why does totalsByTopic sort dictionary keys before returning rows?
options: Swift dictionaries reject repeated keys.
The display contract requires alphabetical order independent of dictionary iteration.
Sorting changes every total into a String.
quiz.explanation: Accumulation and ordering are separate behaviors. Explicit sorting establishes reproducible row order, while the dictionary still stores integer totals.

quiz.question: Why is [10, 0, -2] an incorrect expectation for the supplied numeric fixture?
options: Int never accepts negative strings.
Swift Testing cannot compare arrays.
compactMap omits the nil conversion of bad rather than substituting zero.
quiz.explanation: Int conversion of malformed input yields nil. compactMap drops that element. A validation or zero-substitution policy would need a different API and separate evidence.

workshops.title: Concurrency gates: choose when each request finishes
workshops.summary: Control two requests with explicit signals. Check that old success and old failure cannot change newer state, cancellation keeps live work counted, and shared callers can cancel separately.

simple.story: At a print shop, you first ask for a red poster. Before it is ready, you replace your order with a blue poster. The printer may still finish the red one. The clerk checks the order ticket before putting a poster on your shelf. Only the blue ticket is current. If the old job fails, its error also belongs to the old ticket. Asking the printer to stop does not instantly empty its machine. The clerk keeps that machine counted as busy until the job really ends.
simple.meaning: LatestLoader checks ownership before accepting either a result or an error. CompletionGate lets a test choose exactly when a request starts and finishes. Cancellation requests stopping; current-ticket checks protect visible state even when work continues.

example.before: The selected account is A. An old request is running. A newer request has started and its visible phase is loading.
example.change: Finish the old ignoring gate with ["obsolete"], then wait for its handle before inspecting the loader.
example.after: The visible phase stays loading for the newer ticket. Finish the newer gate with ["current"] and join its handle; the phase becomes loaded for account A with ["current"].

picture.caption: An old response arrives while the newer request still owns the visible state.

items.label: Start old
items.text: Observe the old gate's start signal.

items.label: Start newer
items.text: The newer ticket becomes the current owner.

items.label: Release old
items.text: Its result is rejected and newer loading stays visible.

items.label: Release newer
items.text: Its current result becomes the loaded phase.

words.meaning: A test helper that holds work until the test explicitly supplies a result or error.
A stored way to resume a suspended task, exactly once.
A type that isolates access to its mutable state; it does not own a dedicated thread.
A changing ownership marker that distinguishes separate visits to the same account.
A request for work to stop, which the work must observe or otherwise handle.
One caller waiting for a shared operation's result.

simple.remember: Old work can finish, but only the current owner may change the visible state.
simple.boundary: A print ticket explains ownership, not task scheduling. An actor can handle other calls while one operation awaits. Cancelling a task does not guarantee immediate exit, and a shared caller can receive success if completion wins the cancellation race. These host gates exercise chosen schedules, not real networking.

sections.title: Wait for a signal, then choose the answer
sections.html:
A gate holds a request until the test chooses its answer. CompletionGate lets you observe start, then call succeed or fail. This resembles an Android fake using CompletableDeferred to control an answer. It avoids guessing with sleeps or Task.yield. A continuation stores the way to resume the suspended run operation. The gate is an actor, so changes to that mutable state are isolated. Actor isolation does not give it a dedicated thread. @Sendable and Sendable describe what can safely cross concurrency boundaries; they do not make every shared mutation safe or guarantee that work ends. Sessions 016 and 069 explain those requirements. Each gate accepts one run and one resolution.

Set up the shell function from README with caches under /private/tmp and run the following focused suites. Each suite creates its own actors, so parallel tests cannot share one pending gate by accident. A separate executable mode also demonstrates B surviving an old error; it is a program demonstration, not an assertion suite.

lab_swift test --filter GateTests
lab_swift test --filter LatestLoaderTests
lab_swift test --filter SharedRefreshTests
lab_swift run swift-workbench gates

run marks the operation started and resumes any start observers, then suspends through a checked throwing continuation. succeed carries a value; fail carries an error. Both require a started, unresolved operation. Repeating completion throws alreadyResolved, and repeating run throws alreadyStarted. Resuming a continuation twice is a programming error, so the actor centralizes the transition and clears the stored continuation before delivering it. Swift's checked continuation helps diagnose misuse; it does not design cancellation for you.

CancellationPolicy.cooperative resolves with CancellationError when cancellation is observed. CancellationPolicy.ignore deliberately models an adapter that keeps running after its owner cancels. That policy is essential for freshness testing: otherwise cooperative cancellation could conceal a missing stale-result guard. Event observers return immediately if the event already happened. They are simple test observation helpers without a general cancellation/deadline contract. Resolution means the result was delivered to the suspended continuation, not that a loader already processed it. Await a handle or caller task before asserting terminal state. A test that forgets to release an ignoring gate may hang; the suite time limit is a diagnostic aid, not a substitute for finishing every owned operation.

sections.title: Let only the current request change the screen state
sections.html:
A request ticket records who may accept an answer. LatestLoader tracks the visible phase, such as loading or loaded. start creates a RequestTicket containing the account, account epoch, and request generation, sets loading, and keeps a task alive after start returns. It also returns a handle so you can wait for that task to end. An epoch changes when account ownership changes; a generation distinguishes requests within that ownership. This differs from session 020's caller-owned repository, where load returns or throws directly to its caller. Here a current ordinary error becomes a failed phase; waiting on the handle does not throw it. This example has no cache, TTL, durable writes, retries, or real credentials.

Before finishing, the task enters the loader actor again. finish first removes the tracked task, then validates the entire ticket against current ownership and the account epoch. Both success and failure pass through the same guard before changing the phase, with no intervening await. Actor isolation alone would not supply this guarantee: during the service suspension, another start or changeAccount may execute. A stale success can replace new data, and a stale catch can remove a new loading indicator or display the wrong error. Both paths need evidence.

let loader = LatestLoader(account: "A", cancelSuperseded: false)
let old = CompletionGate<[String]>(cancellationPolicy: .ignore)
let new = CompletionGate<[String]>(cancellationPolicy: .ignore)
let first = try await loader.start(using: old)
await old.waitUntilStarted()
let second = try await loader.start(using: new)
await new.waitUntilStarted()
try await new.succeed(["B"])
await second.wait()
try await old.fail(GateFailure.synthetic("old A"))
await first.wait()
let state = await loader.snapshot()

Request labels A and B describe ordering in this schedule; the selected synthetic account remains A. Disabling cancelSuperseded ensures the old operation remains live independently of cancellation. The tests parameterize old success versus old error and exercise both B-already-loaded and B-still-loading schedules. Assertions check whole phases rather than only the number of returned strings. If you change the catch guard, the old-error case should expose it; increasing a delay cannot repair the ownership rule.

changeAccount increments the epoch, clears ownership and visible state, resets request numbering, and requests cancellation of tracked work. Returning from A to B to A restores the account text but not the previous epoch. The account-cycle tests deliberately give both A requests generation one, release the earlier A while the newer A is still loading, and prove it cannot commit. Comparing account text or request number alone would fail this case. Sessions 015, 016, and 020 provide the cancellation, actor-reentrancy, and ownership groundwork; session 012 explains why these event schedules are stronger than timing guesses.

sections.title: Keep cancelled work counted until it ends
sections.html:
Cancellation asks work to stop. LatestLoader's cancel(ticket) also retires that ticket's right to change visible state. If the ticket is current, the owner clears it and shows idle immediately, then requests task cancellation. The underlying work may still be running. Waiting with handle.wait gives another task a way to join the request; it does not transfer ownership of the retained request. Cancelling that waiting task therefore does not call the loader's cancel API. Keep these actions separate: stop accepting this result, request that work stop, and wait for work to actually exit. A UI caller needs to know which owner controls each action.

The model counts all retained tasks, including superseded requests and canceled ignoring gates. maximumActiveWork is a positive bound on that count. When capacity is reached, start throws capacityReached before changing visible phase, current ticket, or request generation. It does not pretend that task.cancel synchronously freed a slot. The tests begin two operations, request cancellation through supersession, reject a third while both remain active, release a real slot, start another request, and finally release the oldest operation. Peak tracked activity stays two. Cancellation-aware gates demonstrate the cooperative path separately.

This is a reject-on-capacity policy, not a queue, debounce, rate limiter, fairness guarantee, or bound on final payload memory. A caller can retry after joining completed work, but this lab has no production retry policy. If an adapter never responds to cancellation or completion, a slot remains occupied. The owner can prevent state corruption and additional launch growth; it cannot force arbitrary work to stop. A real implementation must choose transport deadlines and shutdown policy at the appropriate boundary. These are consequences of the contract, not an invitation to silently discard active tasks from accounting.

To change the fixture, use the cancel-and-ignore test first. Keep the gate ignoring cancellation, call cancel after waitUntilStarted, and finish with a distinct old payload. Then repeat with a synthetic error. Idle must survive both, and activeWork must become zero only after handle.wait finishes. To explore capacity, change maximumActiveWork and independently adjust the number of started gates; do not leave the original expected peak as an unexplained magic number. Read a failure by asking whether ownership, phase, or actual active-work accounting broke. An error being swallowed into an empty successful result would be a separate contract defect. Session 018 covers preserving cancellation through real transport adapters; this host fake does not exercise URLSession.

sections.title: Share one refresh while letting callers leave separately
sections.html:
A waiter is one caller waiting for an answer. SharedRefresh gives each waiter a separate continuation while keeping one shared underlying operation, called a flight. A second refresh caller joins the current flight; its own supplied gate never starts. Both callers must want the same operation within one declared scope. One actor instance represents that scope. It has no account-switch or authentication policy. Giving every caller the same Task.value would not, by itself, provide this lab's separate cancellation paths. Shared work still needs a rule for each caller's departure and for when the underlying operation should receive cancellation.

Cancelling one caller schedules removal of its waiter on the actor and resumes that caller with CancellationError. The underlying task continues if any waiter remains. The independent-cancellation tests run this schedule for either caller: register two waiters, await waitUntilWaiterCount(2), cancel one, await that caller's failure, inspect one remaining waiter, release the gate, and obtain success from the survivor. A shared-error test separately proves one ordinary failure reaches both registered callers. When the last waiter cancels, current flight eligibility clears and the underlying task receives cancellation.

An abandoned ignoring flight still consumes active capacity until its gate exits. With the default one-flight limit, a replacement request is rejected during that interval. With two slots, a replacement can coexist with abandoned work; completion uses the original flight identity so a late old error cannot terminate the replacement. This protects both continuation ownership and accounting. The tests release and join all operations, including abandoned fakes. No test depends on a fixed sleep to infer registration or completion.

Cancellation and successful completion can race. The contract uses the actor's handling order: if completion delivers a result before cancellation removes the waiter, that caller may receive success. It does not promise that a concurrent cancel call rewrites a result already delivered. The ordered test avoids ambiguity by awaiting the cancelled caller before releasing the gate. A precancelled caller creates no flight. Callback cancellation bridges still use a short Task to enter the actor; storing continuations and clearing them in one isolated transition prevents duplicate resume. A passing instructor suite proves these chosen schedules on the host. It does not prove every possible scheduler interleaving or complete your learner exercise.

exercise.brief: Add one test that chooses the order of old and new answers. Write the expected phases first, use start signals, and finish every request you started.
steps: Use the README's isolated caches to run GateTests, LatestLoaderTests, and SharedRefreshTests. Record their actual summaries.
Read the schedules where the newer request finishes before the old one, for both old success and old error. Then read the cases where newer loading must stay visible.
Trace account A to B to A. Explain why the later A may reuse request generation one but must have a different epoch.
Change one old payload or error label. Check that newer state stays unchanged, then release every ignoring gate and join every handle.
In a scratch exercise, choose a different maximumActiveWork. Write which start must be rejected while old work still occupies a slot, and check that visible state stays unchanged.
Trace cancellation of each shared waiter. Explain why awaiting the cancelled caller before releasing the gate differs from letting cancellation and success race.
Write and run your own schedule with expected and actual phases. Keep that learner evidence separate from the supplied instructor results.
acceptance: Each request starts only after the test observes its start signal, and completion is explicitly controlled.
Both late success and late error are rejected while newer data is loaded and while newer work is loading.
A to B to A invalidation is justified by epoch, not only account text or request numbering.
Cancelled ignoring work stays counted until exit; rejected starts preserve visible state.
Either refresh waiter can cancel independently, ordinary error reaches both waiters, and abandoned flights are joined.
The report distinguishes this phase owner from a caching repository, transport adapter, and real authentication refresh.
exercise.solution:
Start an old request, then a newer one. Release old A successfully while request B is still loading. Set cancelSuperseded to false and use ignoring gates so the test must prove the ownership check itself. The selected account remains A; B names the newer request, not a different account. After joining the old handle, expect loading for the newer ticket. This addition belongs in a learner scratch Swift Testing target that imports SwiftLanguageLab:

import Testing
import SwiftLanguageLab

@Test func learnerSchedule() async throws {
    let owner = LatestLoader(account: "A", cancelSuperseded: false)
    let old = CompletionGate<[String]>(cancellationPolicy: .ignore)
    let new = CompletionGate<[String]>(cancellationPolicy: .ignore)
    let first = try await owner.start(using: old)
    await old.waitUntilStarted()
    let second = try await owner.start(using: new)
    await new.waitUntilStarted()
    try await old.succeed(["obsolete"])
    await first.wait()
    #expect(await owner.snapshot().phase == .loading(second.ticket))
    try await new.succeed(["current"])
    await second.wait()
    #expect(await owner.snapshot().phase == .loaded(account: "A", values: ["current"]))
}

The intermediate assertion proves an old result cannot clear loading, and the final assertion proves the newer request commits. Replacing old.succeed with old.fail exercises the catch boundary. For shared refresh, two registered waiters represent one active flight; cancel one and await its outcome before releasing success to the other. If all waiters cancel an ignoring gate, capacity remains occupied until you explicitly finish it. Those values are expected outcomes of the defined schedule, not a claim that your new test has been authored or executed.

quiz.question: Why test an old error after a new success?
options: Errors cannot cross actor boundaries.
A stale catch can overwrite current phase just as stale success can.
The test runner always delays catch blocks.
quiz.explanation: Reentrancy allows newer ownership while an old operation awaits. Both success and error must check freshness before committing; actor isolation alone does not validate request identity.

quiz.question: After cancelling an ignoring gate, when may its active-work slot be freed?
options: As soon as cancel returns.
When another account name is selected.
After the operation actually exits and its owner records completion.
quiz.explanation: Cancellation is a request. Removing unresponsive work from accounting would permit unbounded real activity while reporting a misleading low count.

quiz.question: What does cancelling one registered shared-refresh waiter guarantee in the ordered test?
options: That waiter stops, while the other can still receive the shared result.
Every waiter receives CancellationError.
A simultaneous result already delivered is retroactively removed.
quiz.explanation: Each waiter owns a separate continuation. The ordered test waits for cancellation handling before completion; simultaneous cancellation and completion are governed by actor handling order.

workshops.title: Foundation files: check text, dates, and file outcomes
workshops.summary: Use fixed dates, locales, and text to get predictable answers. Check missing, empty, corrupt, and unwritable files separately, then state which device behaviors the host tests cannot prove.

simple.story: A cupboard has three labeled boxes. The first box is missing. The second is present, but its list of contents is empty. The third contains a torn list that you cannot read. If you call all three boxes empty, you lose useful information. You might buy supplies that already exist, or ignore a damaged list. A careful check reports each state separately. When replacing a readable list fails before anything is written, you can still read the old list and decide what to do next.
simple.meaning: FixtureFileStore reports a missing file separately from a decoded document with no topics. Bad bytes produce corruption, while reading or writing can fail for other reasons. Fixed Foundation inputs also make date, locale, and text checks repeatable.

example.before: A new TemporaryWorkspace has no snapshot.json file, so load returns .missing.
example.change: Save PracticeDocument(topics: []), then load it again.
example.after: The result is .value(empty), not .missing. A file now contains a valid version-one document with zero topics. Replacing its bytes with a wrong-type topics field should instead produce corrupt.

picture.caption: Three file states require three different outcomes; these are alternatives, not ordered steps.

items.label: Valid empty file
items.text: A decoded document with topics [] becomes a value.

items.label: Wrong contents
items.text: Malformed JSON or an incompatible field type produces corrupt.

items.label: Cannot read bytes
items.text: An I/O problem other than missing becomes readFailed.

words.meaning: Rules for presenting and interpreting numbers and other text for a region or language.
A step to the next date in a chosen calendar and time zone, which need not span 24 elapsed hours.
A Swift text element that can contain several Unicode scalars, such as a letter with a combining accent.
Text positions counted in UTF-16 code units, as used by Foundation's NSRange.
Turning stored bytes into values that match a specified data shape.
Replacing a file as one operation to help readers avoid partial contents; it is not a full transaction between writers.

simple.remember: A missing file, a valid empty document, and unreadable or corrupt data need different answers.
simple.boundary: The cupboard explains distinct outcomes. A real file can change between operations, and not every write failure preserves old bytes. Atomic replacement does not coordinate two logical writers. Host fixtures also do not prove iOS file protection, backup, or document-provider behavior.

sections.title: Choose the date and locale before calculating
sections.html:
Foundation provides tools for dates, formatted numbers, text, URLs, and files. A locale supplies regional formatting rules; a calendar and time zone tell a date calculation what a day means. Android's java.time, NumberFormat, and java.nio handle related jobs, but their defaults and APIs differ. This workshop names every input that affects interpretation instead of taking the current user's settings. That lets you predict exact fixture results. Session 052 explains Foundation correctness, while sessions 058 and 067 supply the type and error vocabulary. The tests use invented text and newly created temporary files. They use no client container, personal text, or real account data.

Use the isolated-cache function in README from the lab directory. Run FoundationTests to obtain assertions and the executable foundation mode to see a small demonstration. The demonstration prints results; the tests prove particular fixture expectations. Record the installed toolchain and actual command outcomes, and read the Swift Testing summary rather than only the XCTest compatibility preamble.

lab_swift test --filter FoundationTests
lab_swift run swift-workbench foundation

springCivilDaySeconds chooses a Gregorian calendar and the America/New_York timezone. It constructs noon on March 9, 2024 and adds one calendar day, then verifies the end remains noon before measuring the elapsed interval. The named historical spring transition gives 82,800 seconds, not 86,400. That is a tested fixture for civil-day arithmetic, not a rule that days everywhere are twenty-three hours. Adding an elapsed duration answers a different question. The Kotlin analogy is a zoned date-time plus a day versus an instant plus a duration, with API-specific matching and gap policies still needing their own study.

The decimal fixture explicitly chooses en_US for 1,234.50 and de_DE for 1.234,50. Both represent the same Decimal value. A local NumberFormatter is configured for decimal style and two displayed fractional digits; the formatter is not shared mutable global state. The test asserts the numeric value and a locale-aware format/parse round trip. It checks the decimal marker and fractional digits without asserting every byte of a localized presentation string. Locale data can change between operating systems. These known well-formed inputs do not establish strict whole-input validation: NumberFormatter may accept more than a product's grammar allows. Currency scale, rounding, overflow, and authorization are separate domain contracts; formatted text must not become a machine wire representation.

sections.title: Count visible characters and text offsets separately
sections.html:
A visible character can use several encoded units. Swift String contains Character values, each representing an extended grapheme cluster: text kept together as one character, such as a letter and its accent. Kotlin and Java indexing commonly counts UTF-16 code units instead. Swift considers composed é and e followed by a combining acute accent equal as text, even though their UTF-8 bytes differ. This is canonical textual equivalence. Equality therefore does not mean identical encoded bytes. A transport byte limit and an editor's character limit ask different questions. Give each its own test inputs and expected result.

let composed = "é"
let decomposed = "e\u{301}"
let sameText = composed == decomposed // true
let visibleCount = decomposed.count // 1
let byteCount = decomposed.utf8.count // 3

let text = "A👩🏽‍💻B"
if let b = text.range(of: "B") {
    let foundationRange = NSRange(b, in: text)
    let roundTrip = Range(foundationRange, in: text)
    let aligned = FoundationFixtures.isCharacterAligned(foundationRange, in: text)
}

The emoji cluster in that string contains a modifier and a joiner sequence. The complete string has three Characters; B begins at UTF-16 offset eight. NSRange conversion takes the exact source string so Foundation offsets can become the appropriate Swift positions. Converting back can fail for an invalid range, so the result is optional. Do not manufacture an integer Character offset from the NSRange location, and do not reuse positions after changing the underlying string. Sessions 061 and 064 connect collection iteration and mutation with these invalidation concerns.

Conversion and editing policy are distinct. Range(_:in:) establishes whether a Foundation range can be represented in the string; it should not be treated as a blanket guarantee that the endpoints follow the application's Character boundaries. isCharacterAligned additionally builds the set of actual Character indices and endIndex, then requires both endpoints to belong to that set. Including endIndex allows a selection reaching the end of the string. The test rejects an out-of-bounds range and a range covering only the first scalar of a decomposed cluster. It asserts the policy result rather than depending on whether a particular partial conversion happens to succeed.

Building a boundary set scans the text, so repeated large edits need a considered strategy rather than an assumed constant-cost operation. The fixture does not implement normalization for wire storage, confusable-identifier detection, secure search, or a text editor. Change the fixture by adding a distinct emoji-adjacent selection and independently deriving its UTF-16 range from the actual string. Assert both round-trip identity and Character alignment. An observed difference in byte count is useful evidence; it is not permission to log real user text while debugging.

sections.title: Tell missing, empty, and corrupt files apart
sections.html:
A temporary workspace is a directory created just for one test. TemporaryWorkspace puts a UUID-named directory under FileManager's temporaryDirectory. Each file test creates its own workspace and uses defer to clean up only that directory. This allows parallel tests without a shared filename collision. FixtureFileStore uses snapshot.json inside its supplied workspace. A learner's label cannot choose a different path. URL path APIs construct file URLs; URL(string:) interprets URL text and is unsuitable for treating an arbitrary filesystem path as a file URL. The example never reads Documents, Application Support, a company store, or an account cache.

let workspace = try TemporaryWorkspace()
defer { try? workspace.cleanup() }
let store = FixtureFileStore(workspace: workspace)
let absent = try store.load() // .missing
let empty = PracticeDocument(topics: [])
try store.save(empty)
let present = try store.load() // .value(empty)

load reads bytes first. A specifically classified Cocoa missing-file error returns FileLoad.missing. Other I/O errors become readFailed with diagnostic context. The implementation does not call fileExists and then assume a later read will have the same outcome; that separate check would introduce a race. Successfully decoded version-one bytes produce value(document), including an empty topics array. Missing and successful-empty are observably different, which mirrors session 020's distinction between absent cache knowledge and known empty results.

Malformed JSON or a field of the wrong type produces corrupt. A valid document with an unsupported version produces unsupportedVersion instead of masquerading as current data. save rejects unsupported versions too. These explicit errors make a future migration policy possible, but this workshop has no migration implementation and does not automatically discard or repair corrupted bytes. Session 018 supplies the related Codable boundary: decoding is evidence about a particular schema, not proof that the data is valid for every domain use.

The missing/corrupt test first observes missing, saves a successful empty document, reads it, and then replaces the bytes with a malformed synthetic fixture. It requires a typed corrupt outcome. Another fixture writes a numeric topics field and checks corruption, while a version-two document checks the version outcome. To change a fixture, edit only its synthetic bytes in the test and calculate the intended outcome. A valid JSON object can still violate the schema. Inspect the failure category before changing a decoder; catching everything and returning an empty array would erase the distinction the test exists to preserve. Cleanup failures are best-effort in defer, while a dedicated directory test verifies bounded removal and isolation.

sections.title: Check a failed write and say what it proves
sections.html:
An atomic replacement helps readers see a complete file rather than a partly written one. The default writer asks Data.write for that behavior. It does not make a whole read-change-write sequence one transaction, and it does not promise crash durability on every filesystem. Two owners could read the same old document, make different changes, and each replace the file atomically. The later write could lose the earlier change. This host example tests the file boundary. A cross-process account store needs a separate coordination rule. An await after an account freshness check can also allow ownership to change before a later durable write.

The writer is an injected @Sendable throwing closure. One test saves a previous synthetic snapshot, substitutes a writer that throws before writing, attempts a replacement, and checks that the writeFailed outcome is visible and the prior document remains. This proves this injected failure path. It does not promise every failure leaves the filesystem unchanged: a different writer might modify bytes and then throw. That limitation belongs in the contract instead of being hidden by a generic test name. Sessions 065 and 068 explain initialization of that dependency and the escaping closure it retains.

A separate test creates a directory at the exact snapshot.json path. Replacing that directory with atomic file data produces a real filesystem write failure, and reading it as document bytes produces readFailed. The directory remains a directory. This fixture does not depend on chmod being effective for the current user, filling a disk, or altering a real file. The malformed-document fixture likewise lives only in its newly created workspace. Each test cleans up its own temporary directory after success or a thrown path.

Read an issue by separating read failure, decoding corruption, version rejection, and write failure. When changing the injected writer, preserve the assertion that an error remains observable; printing a warning and reporting save success would change the caller contract. When changing valid topics, assert the decoded PracticeDocument rather than merely checking that some file exists. Keep actual run output with your fixture change and explain what that result establishes. Passing the instructor tests proves only the supplied host cases. iOS locked-file protection, backup attributes, document-provider coordination, App Group writers, and device lifecycle need native or device evidence. They are specialist follow-up practice, not simulated host successes or completed learner work.

exercise.brief: Build a small set of invented date, number, text, and file cases. Write each expected answer, run the host checks, and list the device checks still needed.
steps: Record the toolchain. With the README cache setup, run FoundationTests and swift-workbench foundation.
Use the named New York dates to explain 82,800 elapsed seconds. Explain how adding a calendar day differs from adding 86,400 seconds.
Parse the en_US and de_DE fixtures into Decimal 1234.5. Format and parse them again, keeping display text separate from transport data.
Add a Unicode selection case. Derive NSRange from that exact string and check both range conversion and Character alignment.
Save a new synthetic topic and check the decoded document. Then make topics the wrong JSON type and require corrupt.
In separate temporary workspaces, inspect missing, successful empty, unsupported version, unreadable directory, injected write failure, and real write failure.
Record the host commands and outcomes. List device file protection, backup, and coordination between writers as separate pending checks.
acceptance: Locale, Gregorian calendar, and named timezone are explicit inputs, not ambient defaults.
Character count, UTF-16 range, and UTF-8 byte counts are distinguished using synthetic strings.
Every file fixture uses its own temporary directory and bounded cleanup; no client or account files are accessed.
Missing, corrupt, unsupported-version, read-failed, and write-failed outcomes cannot be redefined as successful empty.
An injected pre-write failure preserves the previous snapshot, and a directory obstruction exercises a real I/O failure.
The report identifies the limited atomic-write contract and the device behaviors that remain unverified.
exercise.solution:
Start with a valid empty document. Add the synthetic labels below, save, and require the same document on read-back. Then replace topics with a number. Those bytes are valid JSON, but they cannot decode as a list of strings, so the expected outcome is corrupt. Put this code in a learner function or scratch test that imports Foundation and SwiftLanguageLab:

let workspace = try TemporaryWorkspace()
defer { try? workspace.cleanup() }
let store = FixtureFileStore(workspace: workspace)
let expected = PracticeDocument(topics: ["Cafe\u{301}", "👩🏽‍💻"])
try store.save(expected)
let recovered = try store.load()
// Assert recovered == .value(expected) in your test.
try Data(#"{\"version\":1,\"topics\":7}"#.utf8).write(to: store.file)
do {
    _ = try store.load()
    // Record a failed expectation here: decoding should not succeed.
} catch FileStoreError.corrupt {
    // The bytes are valid JSON but incompatible with [String].
}

The corresponding test should fail if corrupt is replaced with missing or an empty value. The two locale fixtures converge on Decimal 1234.5, the decomposed accent is one Character with three UTF-8 bytes, and the named New York civil day spans twenty-three elapsed hours. The pre-write injection preserves the prior snapshot because it never modifies the file; the directory obstruction independently verifies real read and write failure. Your report should include actual commands and outcomes, while listing device protection and coordinated multi-writer behavior as pending evidence. This worked answer does not execute or complete your changed fixture.

quiz.question: What does Swift equality of composed and decomposed accents imply?
options: Their UTF-8 bytes must be identical.
Their textual values are canonically equivalent, while byte representations can differ.
Each scalar is always a separate Character.
quiz.explanation: String equality respects canonical equivalence. Character count, scalar count, UTF-16 length, and encoded byte count answer different questions.

quiz.question: Why create a directory at snapshot.json for the write-failure fixture?
options: It exercises a real obstruction without depending on chmod, privileges, or disk exhaustion.
Directories are always decoded as empty documents.
It proves all iOS protected files are readable while locked.
quiz.explanation: A directory cannot be atomically replaced as the intended regular document in this fixture. The test uses only a unique temporary workspace and establishes no device file-protection behavior.

quiz.question: What is missing from an atomic replacement when two owners read and modify the same old file?
options: A localized filename.
A larger JSON indentation setting.
A protocol coordinating the logical read-modify-write operations.
quiz.explanation: Complete-file visibility is not logical update serialization. Independent replacements can still lose an update, requiring ownership or transaction coordination suited to the real store.
